title: Fever Driven Out by Fever
story:
He thought the demon was finished. He was wrong, and the mistake cost him more than any blow had.

Krishna threw Jvara down upon the surface of the earth, considering him dead from the grinding of his arms. But released from that grip, the fever-demon of incomparable energy did not leave the field. He entered Krishna's body.

Possessed by fever, Krishna's movements slackened. The victor of enemy cities, the great yogin, had to steady himself again and again with his hand on the ground. Sleep pressed upon him; his steps faltered; his hair stood on end; he sighed and yawned without ceasing. The man who had just crushed a demon in his arms was brought low by the demon's last trick, and it was a long time before he regained his natural state.

Then, knowing himself possessed, Krishna did what no one else could have done: he created a fever of his own. From his own energy the dreadful lord brought forth a second Jvara, a fever terrible to all creatures, made for the destruction of the first. The created fever seized the first Jvara by force, dragged him out of Krishna's body, and presented him before his maker. Thus the fever that had entered Krishna was driven out of him by fever itself.

The angry lord struck Jvara down upon the ground and was about to tear him to pieces. Bewildered, the demon cried out: "O Janardana, it behooves you to protect me!"

And as Krishna's hand was raised, a voice without a body spoke from the sky: "O Krishna, O large-armed Krishna, the delight of the Yadavas, do not kill this Jvara. O sinless one, he is worthy of being protected by you."

So Hari, the lord of the past, the future and the present, the great preceptor of the world, let the fever-demon go. Jvara prostrated himself, his head bowed at Krishna's feet, and said: "O descendant of Yadu, O Govinda, hear what I have to submit. Grant me this one boon, that I alone be the fever in this world, and no other flourish beside me."

"It is proper," said the lord, "to confer a boon on one who prays for it. And you have sought my protection. So be it, Jvara. As before, you will be the only fever. And he whom I have created, let him dissolve back into me."

The fever Krishna had made, the cure that had driven out the disease, dissolved into its source and vanished, as everything made from him returns to him. Then Krishna told the demon how he would range through the world, and gave him one more promise: the man who, having saluted Krishna, attentively reads this account of the great battle will be freed from fever. "So be it," said Jvara, delighted, and saluting his master, he left the battlefield.
reflection: The episode turns on a strange symmetry: fever is driven out by fever, the cure created from the same energy as the disease and then dissolved back into its source. And even the demon who had possessed him, once he asked for protection, was spared: in Krishna's world, even fever is answered when it prays.
next_story_tease: But Jvara was not done: before he left the field, the spared demon would receive the terms of his rule over every living thing.
hero_scene: Krishna, pale and weakened, steadying himself with one hand on the ground while the fever enters him; beside him the dreadful counter-Jvara he has created seizes the first Jvara and drags him from Krishna's body.
